card.kicker: NightShift — frontier AI on Arm CPUs
card.title: Kimi K3 (2.8T) on one Arm CPU
card.subtitle: I ran a 2.8-trillion-parameter model on a single Azure Cobalt 100 (Neoverse-N2) VM, no GPU — and measured exactly why big MoE models are slow on CPU. Every number here is from that machine.

card.title: The wall is compute, not just memory
card.subtitle: The 1.56-bit quant that lets K3 fit in RAM is a codebook gather that is ~27x slower to decode than a normal 4-bit quant. I show it three ways and fix part of it.

card.title: iq1_s decodes 27x slower than q4_K
card.subtitle: In-cache compute-ceiling microbench against the real libggml, one Neoverse-N2 core. i-quants decode through a 2048-entry codebook gather with no i8mm path.

term.title: nightshift@cobalt-100 — quant compute ceiling (in-cache, 1 core)
segments: # STREAM bandwidth on this box = 420 GB/s -> K3's roofline ~19 tok/s,
# but it runs at 2.2. The gap is compute (codebook gather), not memory.

card.title: RAM-resident vs streaming, same Arm silicon
card.subtitle: I built the WASTE 3-bit-VQ container myself from the 1.56 TB native weights (982 GB, ~2h, patched a converter bug) and benchmarked its streaming engine against my RAM-resident model on the same box.

segments: ./waste run --budget 450G k3.waste 'why are LLMs memory-bound on CPUs?'

card.title: Measured. Reproducible. Honest.
card.subtitle: First stable RAM-resident K3 (2.8T) on one Arm CPU node - and the first measurement of why CPU K3 is slow. 44 tok/s on a right-sized MoE. Every claim above is a number from the machine; where a win didn't land, I say so.
